pokemon-type-chart.q1: How many Pokémon types are there?
pokemon-type-chart.a1: There are 18: Normal, Fire, Water, Electric, Grass, Ice, Fighting, Poison, Ground, Flying, Psychic, Bug, Rock, Ghost, Dragon, Dark, Steel and Fairy. Fairy was the last one added, in Pokémon X and Y (2013). The chart on this page is the one used since then.
pokemon-type-chart.q2: How do weaknesses work for a Pokémon with two types?
pokemon-type-chart.a2: Multiply the two. Bulbasaur is Grass and Poison: Fire is ×2 on Grass and ×1 on Poison, so ×2 overall; Grass is ×½ on both, so ×¼. If either type is immune, the result is ×0. That is why a dual type can take ×4 or only ×¼, which a single type never does.
pokemon-type-chart.a3: Both of the Pokémon's types are weak to the move, so it does four times the usual damage. Ice moves on Garchomp (Dragon and Ground) are the best-known example. In battle the game says the move is super effective, the same message as ×2.
pokemon-type-chart.a4: Some do, and this page does not count them. Levitate makes a Pokémon immune to Ground moves, Flash Fire to Fire moves, Thick Fat halves Fire and Ice damage, and Wonder Guard lets only super effective moves hit. Terastallizing in Scarlet and Violet changes the Pokémon's type. Check the Pokémon's ability before you rely on a weakness.
pokemon-type-chart.q5: Is the chart the same in Pokémon GO?
pokemon-type-chart.a5: The same types are strong and weak against each other, but the numbers differ. In Pokémon GO a super effective move does 1.6 times the damage and a resisted one 0.625 times, and there are no immunities: a move the main games block, such as Electric on Ground, does about 0.39 times instead.

pokemon-natures.q1: What does a Pokémon's nature do?
pokemon-natures.a1: It raises one stat by 10 % and lowers another by 10 %. Of the 25 natures, 20 do that and 5 (Hardy, Docile, Serious, Bashful and Quirky) change nothing. HP is never raised or lowered.
pokemon-natures.a2: Raise the stat the Pokémon uses and lower one it does not. Physical attackers usually take Adamant (+Attack, −Sp. Atk) or Jolly (+Speed, −Sp. Atk); special attackers take Modest (+Sp. Atk, −Attack) or Timid (+Speed, −Attack). Bold, Impish, Calm and Careful suit Pokémon that take hits. Brave and Quiet lower Speed, which helps under Trick Room.
pokemon-natures.q3: Can I change a Pokémon's nature?
pokemon-natures.a3: In Sword and Shield and in Scarlet and Violet, a mint (such as an Adamant Mint) changes which stats the nature affects, though the summary still shows the original nature. For breeding, a parent holding an Everstone passes its nature to the egg.
pokemon-natures.q4: How much does a nature change a stat?
pokemon-natures.a4: The stat is multiplied by 1.1 or 0.9 and rounded down. A Speed stat of 120 becomes 132 with Jolly or Timid and 108 with Brave or Quiet. The effect applies to the stat itself, not to the base stat.
pokemon-natures.q5: Why does the chart have a diagonal of neutral natures?
pokemon-natures.a5: The games number natures as 5 × the stat raised + the stat lowered. When both are the same stat, the raise and the drop cancel out, so those five natures sit on the diagonal of the grid and change nothing.

pokemon-type-chart.lead: Find a Pokémon's weaknesses in three steps.
pokemon-type-chart.s1t: Type a name or pick the types
pokemon-type-chart.s1b: Search for a Pokémon by name or Pokédex number, or choose one or two types from the menus.
pokemon-type-chart.s2b: See which move types hit ×4 or ×2, which are resisted and which do nothing.
pokemon-type-chart.s3b: Check what the Pokémon's own types hit hard, or look up any pair in the full chart below.

pokemon-natures.lead: Find the nature you want in three steps.
pokemon-natures.s1b: Choose the stat your Pokémon relies on, such as Attack or Speed.
pokemon-natures.s2b: Choose one it does not use, often Sp. Atk on a physical attacker or Attack on a special one.
pokemon-natures.s3b: The page names the nature and marks it in the grid; the list below has all 25.
